question: A team lead has adopted a habit of splitting every request into stages. Today he needs a three-sentence note telling the team that a meeting has moved. How should he handle it?
options: A) Ask for the note in a single request, since the task is small enough that splitting it adds steps without adding value.
B) Ask for several versions of the note in separate stages, then run one more stage to choose between the versions.
C) Ask for an outline of the note first, approve that outline, and only then request the three sentences themselves.
D) Split it into drafting, then tone review and a final polish, so the habit is applied consistently to all writing tasks.
correct_answers: A) Ask for the note in a single request, since the task is small enough that splitting it adds steps without adding value.
explanations: Correct. Decomposition earns its keep when a task is large, has dependent stages, or needs checking before the next step. A short factual note has none of those properties, so one request is the right shape.
Generating and comparing variants is worth the effort when wording carries real weight, which a routine scheduling note does not.
An outline of a three-sentence note is longer than the note. The checkpoint exists to catch direction errors that are expensive later, and here there is nothing expensive to catch.
Applying the habit uniformly ignores what breaking work up is for. Three sentences can be read and judged at a glance, so the extra stages cost time and return nothing.
